---
title: "From cat to elephant: coding with AI"
---

You've now written several programs completely by hand, and that was on
purpose: you know what a drawing statement is, how coordinates work, and
what tidy code looks like. That makes you ready for the next step. In this
exercise you'll work with an AI for the first time, and you'll use it the
way professionals do: as a tool for generating code, not just as a toy.

The task: take your finished cat program from the last exercise and get an
AI to turn it into a different animal. An elephant, a dog, a penguin,
whatever you like. You won't type the new code yourself. Your job is to
write the instructions, judge the result, and make it work.

## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-first-ai-exercise}

Two different AIs appear in this chapter, and it's worth keeping them apart. The
tutor of this part helps you understand the chapter, with hints and questions.
The exercise further down has an AI of its own that writes complete code from
your prompt, because writing that prompt *is* the exercise.

{{< tutor tutor-introduction >}}

## Writing a good prompt {#sec-prompt}

The message you send to an AI is called a **prompt**, and writing good
prompts is a real skill. Remember the genie in the lamp from the start of
this course: it grants exactly what you say, not what you mean. An AI works
the same way. A vague prompt like "make an elephant" gives the AI room to
guess, and it will guess something, just often not what you had in mind.

A good prompt is precise. It says what you want, what the result has to look
like, and what the AI must not change. Compare:

> Make an elephant.

> Here is a TypeScript program that draws a cat using the p5.js library.
> I am a programming beginner, and this code shows everything I have
> learned so far. Change the program so that it draws an elephant instead.
> Keep the same structure: everything stays inside the `setup` function,
> and the canvas keeps its size of 400 by 500 pixels. Only use the kinds
> of commands that already appear in my code.
>
> [your cat code]

The second prompt tells the AI the language, the library, the structure to
keep, the goal, and, just as important, **your level of knowledge**. The
more clearly you describe your wish, the better the result. This skill,
describing exactly what you want, is the same skill you practice when you
sketch a picture before coding it. Precision is what makes both the
computer and the AI do what you actually want.

Telling the AI that you're a beginner is not embarrassing, it's smart.
Without that information, the AI writes code the way it would for a
professional, full of features you haven't learned yet. Code like that
might even run, but it's useless to you: you can't explain it when you hand
it in, and, much worse, you can't fix it when something is wrong. Code you
don't understand is code you can't control. With the beginner sentence in
your prompt, the AI stays inside what you know, and the result remains
*your* program.

## Show the AI your working code {#sec-context}

The most important part of your prompt is your own cat code. Always paste
it in. Here's why.

The AI cannot see your screen. It doesn't know that you work in a web
playground, that your language is TypeScript, that you draw with the p5.js
library, or that your whole program lives inside one `setup` function. If
you just ask for "code that draws an elephant", the AI will happily produce
something, in some programming language, for some graphics library, in some
structure, and there's a good chance it won't run in your environment
at all.

Your working cat code solves that problem. Code that runs is the most
precise description of your environment that exists: it shows the AI the
exact language, the exact library, and the exact structure that your
playground expects. When the AI sees it, it will answer with code of the
same kind. That's why the rule is: **first make it work, then show it to
the AI.**

## Your exercise: a new animal {#sec-animal}

This exercise has its own AI, and you'll find it in the box below.
Unlike the tutor at the start of this chapter, it doesn't give hints: it
writes code from your prompt, exactly the kind of AI this exercise is
about. If your teacher picks a different AI tool for the class, use that
one instead; the steps stay the same.

{{< tutor tutor-elephant title="Your AI for this exercise" text="This AI writes code from your prompt. Like the genie in the lamp, it grants what you say, not what you mean." cta="Open the exercise AI on novedu.at" >}}

Work like this:

1. Open your finished cat program in the web playground and check that it
   still runs. Copy the whole code with `Ctrl` + `C`.
2. Write your prompt: say which animal you want, what the AI should keep
   (the `setup` function, the canvas size, the p5.js drawing commands), and
   paste your cat code below it.
3. Copy the AI's answer, paste it into the playground in place of your old
   code, and run it.
4. Judge the result. Does it run? Are there red squiggly lines? Does it
   actually look like the animal you asked for? If something is wrong, you
   have two options, and both are part of the job: fix small things
   yourself by adjusting coordinates and colors, or tell the AI in a
   follow-up prompt what it should change.
5. Keep your code formatted before you show or hand in your result. That
   rule doesn't change just because an AI wrote the first draft.

Save your cat code somewhere before you replace it, for example in a text
file, so you can always go back.

One more thing: read the code the AI gives you. You know every command in
it, `rect`, `circle`, `triangle`, `fill`, and friends, so you can follow
what it does. You are the programmer here. The AI types faster than you,
but you decide what is good enough, and you are responsible for the result.
